content: - When \(\Theta = I\), we have \(h^H = h_r^H g\). By invoking the Lindeberg-Lévy central limit theorem [21], we have \(h_r^H g \sim \mathcal{CN}(0, N \varrho_h^2 \varrho_g^2)\) as \(N \to \infty\). As the equivalent channel \(h^H\) is a random variable, the average user received power is given by \(P_u = P\mathbb{E}(|h^H|^2) \to NP \varrho_h^2 \varrho_g^2\). For the case of random phase shifts with \(\theta_n \in [0, 2\pi)\), we have \(h^H = h_r^H \bar{g}\) where \(\bar{g} = \Theta g\). As \(\Theta\) is a unitary matrix, it follows that \(\bar{g}\) has the same distribution as \(g\), i.e., \(\bar{g} \sim \mathcal{CN}(0, \varrho_g^2 I)\). Thus we attain the same result as \(\Theta = I\).

- For optimal \(\Theta\) where the solution is given by (28), we have \(|h^{H}| = |\pmb{h}_{r}^{H}\pmb{\Theta}\pmb{g}| = \sum_{n=1}^{N}|h_{r,n}||g_{n}|\), where \(h_{r,n}\) and \(g_{n}\) are the \(n\)-th elements in \(\pmb{h}_{r}^{H}\) and \(\pmb{g}\), respectively.
